Hybrid Centrality

Source: R/centrality-batch62.R
centrality_hybrid.Rd

Hybrid centrality (Christensen et al. 2018) combines eight rankings of the nodes into one score: $$HC = \frac{BC^w + BC^u + LC^w + LC^u + k^u + EC^w + EC^u + NS^w - 8} {8 (N - 1)},$$ where each term is the rank of the node on one centrality: betweenness (\(BC\)), closeness (\(LC\)) and eigenvector centrality (\(EC\)), each on the weighted (\(w\)) and on the unweighted (\(u\)) network, the degree (\(k\)) and the strength (\(NS\)).

Usage

centrality_hybrid(x, ...)

Arguments

x

Network input accepted by centrality.

...

Further arguments to centrality, such as weighted.

Value

A named numeric vector with one score per node, in input node order, between 0 and 1, or NA at every node when the score is undefined.

Details

The most central node holds the largest rank, and tied nodes share the largest rank of their group. The score runs from 0, for a node last on every centrality, to 1, for a node first on every one. Weights are read as strengths of association, and the length of a path on the weighted network is the sum of the reciprocal weights. On an unweighted network the weighted and unweighted rankings coincide. Loops are ignored.

Betweenness is Freeman's shortest-path betweenness, as the source states. The function hybrid() of the NetworkToolbox package, by the first author, uses randomized shortest paths betweenness unless told otherwise, and rounds every centrality to three decimals before ranking, so its values can differ. Here every centrality is rounded to twelve significant digits before ranking, so that scores equal in exact arithmetic are tied.

The measure is defined for connected undirected networks of at least two nodes. Otherwise every score is NA with a cograph_undefined_measure warning.

References

Christensen, A. P., Kenett, Y. N., Aste, T., Silvia, P. J. and Kwapil, T. R. (2018). Network structure of the Wisconsin Schizotypy Scales-Short Forms: examining psychometric network filtering approaches. Behavior Research Methods, 50(6), 2531-2550. doi:10.3758/s13428-018-1032-9 .

See also

centrality_betweenness, centrality_closeness, centrality_eigenvector, centrality.

Examples

ring <- matrix(0, 5, 5, dimnames = list(letters[1:5], letters[1:5]))
ring[cbind(1:5, c(2:5, 1))] <- c(0.9, 0.2, 0.5, 0.7, 0.4)
ring <- ring + t(ring)
centrality_hybrid(ring)
#>       a       b       c       d       e 
#> 0.90625 0.71875 0.53125 0.81250 0.87500
